units.title: State-machine replication and safety versus liveness
outcomes: Explain how an agreed command prefix and deterministic execution produce replicated state.
Separate election safety, log matching and state-machine safety from conditional progress.
State the crash-recovery, storage and timing assumptions behind your consensus contract.
units.why: The Systems unit on replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary named the pieces. Here the contract becomes a ledger of properties that every later Raft transition must preserve, not another survey of replication styles.

next.note: Turn the contract into election transitions.

study.title: Raft extended paper (20 May 2014): replication contract
study.locator: Section 2, Replicated state machines, and Figure 1; Figure 3, Raft guarantees; Section 5.6, Timing and availability
study.depth: Read the guarantees as obligations to justify later. Skip the Paxos comparison and the evaluation for now.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3: module boundary
study.locator: Introduction, Getting Started and The code, through the description of `labrpc`
study.depth: Inspect the interface and public tests. Begin implementation in the election unit; keep course solutions private.

focus: Replicas at different applied indexes need not have identical current state. Equal initial state and an equal deterministic command prefix imply equal state at that prefix.
Uncommitted suffixes may differ. State-machine safety forbids different commands being applied at the same index, not temporary differences between whole logs.

Basic Raft safety assumes correct protocol execution and stable storage across crashes, not bounded message delay. Progress also needs a communicating majority and sufficiently stable timing and leadership.
A safety counterexample has a finite bad prefix. A bounded interval without commits is evidence of a stall, not a proof of permanent nontermination.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the client, consensus module, log and state machine from Figure 1. Trace an append through local acceptance, durable replication, commitment, application and reply. Mark which boundaries the Lab 3 interface exposes and which belong to the service. Classify a conflicting applied command as a safety violation and a minority partition with no completed writes as a progress stall.
traps: Treating `Start()` returning as a successful client write. It starts agreement; it does not promise commitment.
Putting local randomness or wall-clock reads inside the deterministic application transition instead of agreeing their results as command data.
Reading the paper's availability summary as an unconditional termination theorem for any network with a connected majority. Timing and competing elections still matter.

selfTest.q: Two replicas have applied different-length prefixes. Must their current states match?
selfTest.a: No. Compare state after the same prefix. A lagging replica can be safe while behind.

selfTest.q: Can a safe log contain different commands at one index on different servers?
selfTest.a: Yes, in uncommitted suffixes. They must not both become applied decisions at that index.

selfTest.q: Does a timeout establish that the leader crashed?
selfTest.a: No. It creates suspicion. Safety must survive false suspicion; progress needs additional timing and communication assumptions.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `loglab` invariant ledger, fault-model statement and separate acceptance, persistence, commit, apply and reply events.
units.stopWhen: Your ledger names a finite witness for each safety property and states the assumptions needed for progress without requiring identical uncommitted logs.

fit.note: The paper supplies the precise contract and timing boundary; the lab interface and mini-project make the abstraction boundaries observable.

units.title: Terms and epochs, follower, candidate and leader states and randomized election timeouts
outcomes: Implement follower, candidate and leader transitions with monotonic terms.
Justify at most one elected leader per term using persistent votes and majority intersection.
Diagnose repeated elections without weakening voting rules.
units.why: The election state machine establishes authority for one term. Randomized timeouts help establish that authority promptly; they do not make conflicting votes safe.

next.note: Add log freshness and examine election recovery.

study.title: Raft extended paper: election state machine
study.locator: Sections 5.1 and 5.2; Figure 2 election state and rules; Figures 4 and 5

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3A: leader election
study.locator: Part 3A: leader election, including heartbeat limits and election timeout guidance

focus: On an election timeout, increment the term, vote for yourself, reset the randomized election timer and send vote requests. Count distinct voters only for the election still in progress.
In basic Raft, a higher term in either an RPC request or response makes a candidate or leader update its term and become a follower. A stale response must not resurrect an old election.
A candidate receiving same-term AppendEntries becomes a follower. A term need not elect any leader, and servers need not observe term changes simultaneously.
Reset election timers for the Figure 2 events, not every incoming packet. Choose timeout and heartbeat spacing for the lab's limits rather than copying the paper's example milliseconds.
units.reproduce: From a blank page, trace three followers in term 0. Let one time out, enter term 1, vote for itself and receive a second distinct vote: it becomes leader. Deliver that second vote again: the count must not increase. Then deliver a response carrying term 2: the leader becomes a term-2 follower. Implement this transition trace alongside Lab 3A on your machine.
traps: Claiming there can never be two servers that think they are leader. The invariant is one elected leader per term, not instant agreement across terms.
Resetting the timer on a rejected stale vote request, allowing an obsolete sender to suppress progress.
Reading replies after unlocking and applying them without checking that the role and term still match the RPC's election.

selfTest.q: Why can two different candidates not each win term 7 in a fixed configuration?
selfTest.a: Their majorities intersect, and the intersecting server cannot vote for both in term 7, including across a restart.

selfTest.q: Does a candidate step down on same-term AppendEntries?
selfTest.a: Yes. It recognizes the elected leader for that term. A stale-term AppendEntries is rejected instead.

selfTest.q: Do identical election timeouts threaten safety or progress?
selfTest.a: Progress: simultaneous candidates may repeatedly split the vote. Correct majority and one-vote rules still preserve election safety.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3A: leader election
practice.locator: Part 3A; `TestInitialElection3A`, `TestReElection3A` and `TestManyElections3A`; run `make RUN="-run 3A" raft1` from `src`
practice.note: Use the public tests locally with Go and the race detector through the supplied Make target. They exercise initial election and elections under disconnection and reconnection, not disk durability. Keep solutions private.

units.stopWhen: Lab 3A passes, and your explicit trace ignores a duplicate vote and steps down on a higher-term reply without accepting delayed votes from the old election.

fit.note: The paper derives election safety and the lab provides bounded local implementation practice with public network-failure tests.

units.title: The RequestVote freshness rule, split votes, pre-vote and leadership transfer
outcomes: Implement the term-first, index-second vote freshness comparison.
Walk a split vote through a later successful election without double voting.
Explain what pre-vote and leadership transfer change, and which safety checks they retain.
units.why: Election safety alone can elect a server missing committed history. Freshness connects election to log safety; the optional mechanisms address avoidable disruptions rather than replacing that rule.

next.note: Preserve matching prefixes when the elected leader replicates.
Use freshness in the leader-completeness argument.

study.title: Raft extended paper: election restriction
study.locator: Section 5.4.1, Election restriction; Section 5.2 paragraphs on split votes; Figure 2 RequestVote receiver rules

study.title: Ongaro's 2014 thesis: optional election mechanisms
study.locator: Section 3.10, Leadership transfer extension; Section 9.6, Preventing disruptions when a server rejoins the cluster
study.depth: Explain both extensions; implementation is optional. Do not implement the thesis's election simulator or reproduce its performance results.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: election prerequisite
study.locator: Part 3B: log, instruction to implement the Section 5.4.1 election restriction
study.depth: Add freshness to the existing election code. Finish replication in the following units.

focus: Compare `lastLogTerm` first, then `lastLogIndex` only when terms tie. Neither total log length nor the candidate's election term substitutes for its last entry's term.
Freshness is necessary but not sufficient for granting a vote: the request term and the recorded vote still constrain the decision.
Pre-vote asks whether a prospective election could win before incrementing the local term. An isolated node cannot repeatedly advance its term just by timing out under this extension.
Leadership transfer catches up the target, stops accepting new work during transfer and triggers a normal new-term election with `TimeoutNow`. It does not appoint a leader without votes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compare logs by their last entry. A voter ends at index 10 in log term 3. A candidate ending at index 6 in log term 4 passes freshness; one ending at index 20 in log term 2 fails; one ending at index 9 in log term 3 fails. Assume the RPC election term is acceptable and no other vote was cast. Then draw a three-candidate split vote and a later term in which one candidate obtains two distinct votes.
traps: Granting a vote to a longer log whose last entry has an older term.
Treating a pre-vote response as a durable vote or changing the current term merely because a prospective term is mentioned.
Assuming pre-vote cures all membership disruptions or guarantees progress under arbitrary partitions. It addresses a particular rejoining-node disruption.

selfTest.q: A candidate has the same last log term and index as the voter. Is freshness satisfied?
selfTest.a: Yes. Equality passes freshness, but the voter must still satisfy the term and one-vote rules.

selfTest.q: Why may a shorter log be more up-to-date?
selfTest.a: Its last entry can have a newer term. Raft orders by last term before length; commitment safety also relies on the current-term commit restriction.

selfTest.q: Can leadership transfer succeed if the target cannot obtain a majority?
selfTest.a: No. The target must win an ordinary election. The proposed transfer aborts if it does not complete, rather than bypassing quorum rules.

practice.name: Cambridge Concurrent and Distributed Systems notes: Exercise 18
practice.locator: Exercise 18, end of Section 6: three nodes' Raft logs, parts (a) to (d)
practice.note: Answer part (c) with the freshness rule now; return to part (b) after the commitment unit and part (d) after the repair unit. The notes use their own Raft pseudocode with `commitLength`, so translate to the paper's `commitIndex`. Pre-vote and transfer schedules stay with the section mini-project.

units.stopWhen: Your vote handler passes the three freshness cases, your split-vote trace recovers in a later term, and you can explain the optional extensions without treating them as new authority rules.

fit.note: The paper and lab supply freshness; the existing thesis companion fills the pre-vote and transfer gap, with implementation practice in the mini-project.

units.title: The AppendEntries consistency check and the log matching property
outcomes: Derive log matching by induction over successful AppendEntries transitions.
Implement predecessor checks and idempotent appends for empty and nonempty RPCs.
Track replication evidence separately from the next position to try.
units.why: AppendEntries establishes a matching prefix, not just receipt of a message. That prefix is the evidence later used to advance commitment safely.

next.note: Repair a rejected prefix without damaging matching entries.

study.title: Raft extended paper: prefix agreement
study.locator: Section 5.3, Log replication, through the Log Matching Property argument; Figure 2 AppendEntries receiver and leader rules; Figure 6

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: basic agreement
study.locator: Part 3B: log, from `Start()` and `TestBasicAgree3B` through the election restriction
study.depth: First reach basic agreement. Complete the repair and commitment cases in the next two units before claiming all of 3B is finished.

focus: Reject when `prevLogIndex` is absent or its term differs from `prevLogTerm`. A heartbeat is still AppendEntries and must run this check.
One leader per term creates at most one command at each index in that term. The predecessor check then extends the identical-prefix property inductively.
Successful replication proves agreement only through the request's last entry, or its predecessor for an empty request. Extra follower entries beyond that boundary are not evidence of agreement.
`matchIndex` is confirmed replication evidence; `nextIndex` is a sending cursor that may move backward. Do not count the cursor as a successful acknowledgement.
units.reproduce: Use 1-based log indexes and an agreed term-0 sentinel at index 0. The follower's entry terms are `[1, 1, 2]`. An RPC with predecessor index 3, predecessor term 3 and no entries must fail without modifying the log. An RPC with predecessor index 2, predecessor term 1 and one term-3 entry at index 3 succeeds and leaves `[1, 1, 3]`. Replay it: the log is unchanged. Explain the induction step without looking at Figure 2.
traps: Returning success immediately for an empty heartbeat, then letting the leader infer a prefix that was never checked.
Advancing the follower commit boundary beyond the last index established by this request because the follower happens to have a longer suffix.
Inferring matching prefixes from equal terms alone, ignoring the index and the protocol assumptions that made the entry unique.

selfTest.q: Does an empty AppendEntries prove that the whole follower log matches?
selfTest.a: No. If successful it establishes a matching prefix through its predecessor index, not agreement on an unchecked suffix.

selfTest.q: What happens when the predecessor index exists but its term differs?
selfTest.a: Reject the RPC without appending or truncating. Repair follows a later request whose predecessor matches.

selfTest.q: Why does delivering the same successful append twice not duplicate commands in the log?
selfTest.a: Entries already present at the same indexes with matching terms are retained. Only missing entries are appended.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: basic agreement
practice.note: The public test checks three submitted commands agree at consecutive indexes. Add your own empty-RPC rejection and duplicate-delivery cases; this test alone does not establish log matching for adversarial histories.

units.stopWhen: Basic agreement passes, the fixed rejection and duplicate traces match, and your prefix proof explains why the same checks apply to heartbeats.

fit.note: Section 5.3 provides the induction argument and Figure 2 the implementation contract; Lab 3B plus mini-project traces supply practice.

units.title: Conflict truncation, log repair and slow-follower backtracking
outcomes: Implement first-conflict truncation while retaining matching suffix entries not contradicted by a request.
Use rejection hints to backtrack by conflicting term rather than one index at a time.
Diagnose slow catch-up using rejected requests and replication cursors.
units.why: Leaders inherit followers with missing, extra and conflicting suffixes. Repair must tolerate reordered requests without turning an optimization into a destructive log rewrite.

next.note: Establish why repaired entries cannot replace committed history.

study.title: Raft extended paper: divergent suffix repair
study.locator: Section 5.3, follower inconsistencies and `nextIndex` repair, pp. 7 to 8; Figure 7; Figure 2 receiver rules 2 to 4

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B and 3C: backtracking
study.locator: Part 3B: `TestBackup3B`; Part 3C: the `XTerm`, `XIndex`, `XLen` rejection-hint example
study.depth: Read only the backtracking guidance from 3C here. Implement persistence in its own unit.

focus: After a matching predecessor, compare incoming entries in order. Delete the follower suffix only at the first same-index, different-term conflict, then append the remaining incoming entries.
A short delayed request that matches existing entries must not truncate the follower merely because the request ends earlier than the log.
If the leader lacks the conflicting term, jump to its first follower index. If it has that term, try after the leader's last entry of that term. A too-short follower needs a separate length hint.
Tie reply handling to the relevant leader term and request. A delayed rejection must not undo newer confirmed progress or cause an endless backward/forward loop.
units.reproduce: With 1-based entries and a sentinel at index 0, let the leader's term sequence be `[1, 1, 4, 4]` and the follower's `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]`. A check at predecessor index 4 fails with conflicting term 2, first index 3. Since the leader lacks term 2, retry from index 3 using predecessor index 2, term 1. The follower becomes `[1, 1, 4, 4]`. Now deliver a shorter matching request ending at index 3: index 4 must remain.
traps: Truncating to the predecessor on every successful request, including duplicates and empty heartbeats.
Using a length hint without documenting whether it includes the sentinel; translate it to an absolute next log index.
Letting one slow follower block replication to all others. Send and track follower work independently.

selfTest.q: The leader has the follower's conflicting term. Where does the optimized retry start?
selfTest.a: Immediately after the leader's last entry in that term. The next predecessor check still decides whether the prefix actually matches.

selfTest.q: A duplicate request contains no conflict but ends before the follower log. May it delete the tail?
selfTest.a: No. Ending the request is not evidence of a conflicting entry. Retain the tail until an actual conflict is supplied.

selfTest.q: Does a rejection-hint optimization change which histories can be committed?
selfTest.a: No. It changes where the next consistency check starts, not the checks, election restrictions or commitment rules.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: fast backup
practice.note: The test builds long uncommitted suffixes in minority partitions, commits in other majorities, then reconnects all servers for agreement. Keep your own shorter-request regression too. Finish the whole 3B suite after the commitment unit.

units.stopWhen: The fixed repair trace retains index 4 after the shorter request, and `TestBackup3B` passes without changing the public tests or the prefix check.

fit.note: The paper supplies safe repair and the lab handout fills in the hint cases; the public backup test exercises divergent suffix recovery.

units.title: Majority commitment, the current-term restriction, committed-entry preservation and leader completeness
outcomes: Construct the counterexample to committing an older-term entry by replica count alone.
Derive leader completeness from quorum intersection, freshness, log matching and current-term commitment.
Explain why committing a current-term entry also commits the preceding prefix.
units.why: A majority of copies is not a complete Raft commit rule. Figure 8 is the counterexample that connects the voting restriction to committed-entry preservation.

next.note: Preserve the proof's state across crashes and apply only the committed prefix.

study.title: Raft extended paper: commitment and safety proof
study.locator: Sections 5.4.1 to 5.4.3; Figures 8 and 9; Figure 2 leader commit rule

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: finish log agreement
study.locator: Part 3B: log, including `TestFailNoAgree3B` and the full 3B test list

focus: The leader advances commitment by counting replication only at an index whose entry term equals its current term. Older entries become committed indirectly as part of that prefix.
Intersection supplies a voter that saw the committed entry; freshness and log matching explain why that voter cannot elect the first later leader missing it. Intersection alone is not the proof.
Keep each entry's original term during retransmission. A new leader cannot relabel an old entry to evade the current-term restriction.
A follower learning a larger leader commit index advances only through the prefix established by that AppendEntries. Apply never runs ahead of local commitment.
units.reproduce: Redraw Figure 8(a) through (d) closed-book, recording each server's log terms and the votes that allow the term-3 log to win after the older entry reached a majority in term 4. Explain why counting that older entry as committed was invalid. Then draw branch (e): a term-4 entry reaches a majority and commits the prefix. Identify the intersecting voter in Figure 9 and explain both last-log-term cases in the contradiction proof.
traps: Calling any majority-replicated old entry committed. The creator's term and the current leader's term are different cases.
Assuming a newly elected leader already knows its full committed prefix. Possessing entries and knowing which are committed are separate facts.
Asserting that the paper's Figure 8 test is a proof. Random leader failures sample related histories; the explicit counterexample and invariant argument still matter.

selfTest.q: A term-6 leader has an entry from term 4 on three of five servers. Can that count alone commit it?
selfTest.a: No. The leader must commit a term-6 entry by majority replication, thereby committing the older prefix indirectly.

selfTest.q: Why does a committed term-6 entry protect earlier entries in its log?
selfTest.a: Leader completeness preserves that entry on future leaders, and log matching preserves its entire prefix.

selfTest.q: Is a lost quorum permission to acknowledge writes locally?
selfTest.a: No. The leader may accept uncommitted proposals, but cannot acknowledge them as committed under the majority contract.

units.title: Ordered exactly-once application, persistent term, vote and log state, and crash and restart
outcomes: Persist term, vote and log changes before issuing replies that rely on them.
Restore application state and its applied boundary consistently across restart.
Distinguish once-per-index application from deduplication of retried client operations.
units.why: Crash recovery is part of the consensus proof. A vote forgotten after a restart can invalidate election safety even when every live transition looked correct.

next.note: Extend protection beyond the replicated state machine.
Persist a compacted application prefix with its recovery boundary.

study.title: Raft extended paper: durable protocol state and client retries
study.locator: Figure 2 persistent state and application rule; Section 5.5, Follower and candidate crashes; Section 8 client serial numbers and cached responses
study.depth: Stop before Section 8 read-only queries; read paths have their own unit.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3C: persistence
study.locator: Part 3C: persistence, `persist()`, `readPersist()`, `ReadRaftState()` and `Save()`, and the 3C tests

focus: Persist `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and log updates before replying to RPCs that rely on the changes. Reload them before processing new traffic after restart.

Apply committed entries in increasing index order. Replaying the log into fresh volatile application state is legitimate; reapplying it to already durable effects without a matching applied boundary is not.

If application state survives restart, its applied index must survive consistently with it. Reuse the crash-consistent publication boundary from the storage section, rather than independently saving two unrelated values.

The same client operation can occupy several log indexes after retry. Durable client identity, sequence state and cached replies suppress duplicate logical effects inside the replicated application; they do not make an external API call atomic with the log.
units.reproduce: Draw a voter granting a term-5 vote to one candidate, crashing after the reply, and receiving another candidate's term-5 request after restart. With the saved vote it rejects; without it, a second vote can let two majorities elect different leaders. Then trace an increment committed and applied before a lost client reply. Show why a retry at another log index increments twice without client deduplication, but returns the saved result without another increment when deduplication state and application state recover together.
traps: Calling Lab 3C a test of disk flush or power-loss behavior. Its `Persister` simulates retained bytes; `loglab` must test the actual durable boundary separately.
Persisting an applied index before the corresponding application update, or persisting the update but forgetting its applied index.
Dropping duplicate-suppression state during snapshot or restart, then claiming exactly-once client semantics.

selfTest.q: Why is saving a granted vote after sending the reply unsafe?
selfTest.a: A crash in between can erase the vote and permit a second vote in the same term, breaking the intersection argument.

selfTest.q: Does once-per-index application imply once-per-client-request execution?
selfTest.a: No. A retried request may appear at another index. The application needs a stable request identity and recovered deduplication state.

selfTest.q: Can the paper's volatile applied index be reset on restart?
selfTest.a: Yes if the application is rebuilt from a consistent snapshot or fresh state with the corresponding replay boundary. It is unsafe to replay old effects into retained application state without coordinating that boundary.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3C: retained-state recovery
practice.locator: Part 3C; `TestPersist13C`, `TestPersist23C`, `TestPersist33C`, `TestFigure83C` and the remaining 3C tests; run `make RUN="-run 3C" raft1` from `src`
practice.note: The persistence tests crash and restart servers while agreement continues; Figure 8 stress repeatedly crashes leaders and finally asks all servers to agree. Preserve these public results separately from `loglab` storage-crash and client-retry evidence.

units.stopWhen: Lab 3C passes with 3A and 3B still passing, and your recovery ledger covers both the vote-before-reply window and the application-state/deduplication boundary.

fit.note: Figure 2 and Section 8 distinguish protocol and application persistence; Lab 3C checks simulated recovery and the mini-project adds durable crash injection.

units.title: Leader partitions, stale messages and fenced locks
outcomes: Walk an old leader's partition, higher-term replacement and delayed-message rejection.
Build a fenced lock using committed acquisition order and a resource-side enforcement boundary.
State precisely when a stale holder loses permission to affect the protected resource.
units.why: The earlier unit on leases, process pauses and fencing tokens showed why a lease alone cannot protect a resource. Raft protects its log from stale authority; a protected file or service needs its own enforcement, not faith in the client's lease checks.

next.note: Prevent an isolated old leader from serving stale reads too.
Carry fenced ownership into shard movement.

study.title: Raft extended paper: obsolete authority
study.locator: Section 5.1 term comparison; Figure 2 all-server higher-term rule and stale-term RPC rejection; Section 8 isolated-leader read hazard

study.title: How to do distributed locking (8 February 2016): resource enforcement
study.locator: Protecting a resource with a lock; Making the lock safe with fencing, including tokens 33 and 34
study.depth: Use the pause and fencing derivation. Skip the dated Redlock implementation critique.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: consensus-backed coordination
study.locator: Chapter 10, Consistency and Consensus: Using shared logs, pp. 433 to 434; Coordination Services, pp. 437 to 438
study.depth: Read the shared-log counter and the coordination-service features, not the intervening protocol survey.

focus: An old leader can remain unaware of replacement. It cannot commit alone, but a client that already holds a token can still send external requests.

Issue each acquisition token from committed, applied lock state. An acquisition's log index can distinguish acquisitions within one term; a term alone cannot distinguish successive holders in that term.
At the protected resource, atomically check the token and update the remembered maximum with the effect. Persist that maximum consistently with the effect across restart.

A remembered maximum rejects an older token after a higher token has reached the resource, not immediately when a lease expires elsewhere. For revocation before new-owner activation, add an authoritative ownership check or an explicit fencing-installation handshake.
units.reproduce: Trace the essay's order: holder 1 pauses with token 33; holder 2 acquires token 34 and the resource accepts its write; holder 1 resumes and its token-33 write is rejected. Restart the resource from its durable token and effect state and reject token 33 again. Reverse the two resource arrivals and explain why a maximum-token check alone cannot know that token 34 was granted but has not arrived. Keep the two guarantees separate.
traps: Returning a token for an uncommitted proposal. Its log position may be overwritten or reused for another command.
Treating a fencing token as a request-deduplication key. Several authorized writes may share a holder token; retries need their own identity.
Checking ownership at the client before an external write. A pause or delayed packet can occur after the check.

selfTest.q: Why is the leader term alone insufficient as a lock-acquisition token?
selfTest.a: Multiple acquisitions can occur in one leader term. They need distinct ordered tokens, such as their committed acquisition indexes.

selfTest.q: Must equal-token writes always be rejected?
selfTest.a: No. A holder may make several writes. Define the equal-token policy and separately deduplicate request IDs; reject tokens older than the installed maximum.

selfTest.q: Does token 34 being granted instantly make token 33 fail at an uninformed resource?
selfTest.a: No. The resource must learn the higher token or validate current authority. A local maximum-token check cannot infer an unseen grant.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a committed `loglab` lock acquisition, resource-side fencing with durable token state, stale-holder replay and an explicit new-owner activation boundary.
units.stopWhen: The delayed old-holder effect fails after higher-token installation and after resource restart, and your contract explicitly covers the gap between grant and resource activation.

fit.note: The paper covers stale protocol messages; the locking essay and DDIA connect committed order to resource fencing, exercised by the mini-project.

units.title: Snapshot creation, log compaction and snapshot installation
outcomes: Create a snapshot of an applied committed prefix with its index, term and application recovery state.
Install snapshots without regressing application state or retaining a conflicting suffix.
Recover a consistent snapshot and log tail after a crash.
units.why: Compaction removes the very entries used by prefix checks and replay. The snapshot must replace both their state and the metadata needed to connect the surviving tail.

next.note: Include configuration state in the recoverable prefix.

study.title: Raft extended paper: snapshot boundary
study.locator: Section 7, Log compaction; Figures 12 and 13
study.depth: Understand chunked installation but implement one whole-snapshot RPC as Lab 3D requires. Incremental compaction and copy-on-write optimization are not required.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3D: log compaction
study.locator: Part 3D: log compaction, including `Snapshot()`, `InstallSnapshot`, restart application ordering and `persister.Save()`

focus: Snapshot only state through an applied committed index. Keep the last included index and term as the predecessor anchor for the first retained entry.
Use absolute log indexes after compaction and translate them to local storage offsets in one place. An array offset is no longer the protocol index.
Retain the suffix after an installed snapshot only if the local entry at its boundary has the same index and term. Do not let a delayed snapshot roll back an already newer applied state.
Recover snapshot data, boundary metadata, client deduplication state and any configuration consistently. Publish the replacement durably before deleting the recovery data it supersedes.
units.reproduce: Draw a snapshot through index 5 whose last included term is 2. The next AppendEntries anchor is index 5, term 2 even though entries 1 through 5 are no longer stored as ordinary entries. For installation, compare a follower that has that same boundary and a tail against one whose entry at index 5 has a different term: retain the first tail, discard the conflicting one. Finally trace a delayed snapshot older than the service's applied boundary and show that application state does not move backward.
traps: Snapshotting the log's last index even though the application has not applied that prefix.
Saving new boundary metadata with old snapshot contents, producing a recovery image that claims effects it does not contain.
Passing a missing snapshot to a later persistence update after compaction and thereby losing the saved application prefix.

selfTest.q: Why retain the last included term after deleting the prefix?
selfTest.a: It supplies the predecessor term for consistency checks immediately after the snapshot boundary.

selfTest.q: May a follower keep an uncommitted tail when the snapshot boundary conflicts?
selfTest.a: No. That tail is not anchored to the installed prefix and must be discarded. A matching boundary permits retaining the following tail.

selfTest.q: Does a successful Lab 3D run demonstrate atomic disk publication?
selfTest.a: No. It exercises the lab's simulated persistence. Actual partial snapshot and publication crashes need the durable-storage tests in `loglab`.

units.title: Membership change safety and joint consensus
outcomes: Construct disjoint old and new majorities under an unsafe direct configuration switch.
Derive the separate-majority predicate for joint elections and commitment.
Optionally implement a serialized joint-consensus transition with crash and snapshot recovery.
units.why: The earlier quorum arguments assumed one fixed voter universe. Reconfiguration must preserve the argument while servers learn about the change at different times.

next.note: Require read confirmation under the applicable voter configuration.
Separate consensus voter changes from ownership movement.

study.title: Raft extended paper: joint membership transition
study.locator: Section 6, Cluster membership changes; Figures 10 and 11

study.title: Ongaro's 2014 thesis: joint-consensus algorithm
study.locator: Section 4.3, Arbitrary configuration changes using joint consensus, including Figure 4.8
study.depth: Use this variant consistently for the optional implementation. Do not mix its configuration activation rules with the thesis's single-server variant or a library's different activation rule.

focus: Joint consensus needs a majority of the old configuration and a majority of the new one, for elections and commitment. A majority of their union is not equivalent.

In this paper's variant a server uses the latest configuration stored in its log, even before commitment. Commit the joint configuration under both majorities before proposing the new-only configuration.
Catch up new servers as nonvoters before changing the voter set. A removed leader steps down when the new-only entry commits; it cannot count itself in a configuration that excludes it.
Serialize configuration changes and preserve configuration state through snapshots and restart. Voter membership is protocol state, not an independently edited discovery list.
units.reproduce: Take old voters A, B, C and new voters C, D, E. Under a direct switch, A and B form an old majority while D and E form a disjoint new majority. Under joint consensus, A, B, C is a majority of the union but fails the new majority. A, C, D satisfies both. Enumerate the subsets by hand or with Python 3 and verify these verdicts, then trace joint commitment followed by new-only commitment with a leader crash between them.
traps: Waiting to activate the joint entry until it commits while otherwise following the paper's activate-on-storage algorithm.
Removing a failed voter locally just to restore a majority. This changes the quorum universe without the required transition.
Assuming MIT Lab 3 tests membership changes. The handout explicitly excludes Section 6.

selfTest.q: Why is a majority of the union insufficient for the two three-voter configurations?
selfTest.a: A, B, C has three of the five union members but only C from the new configuration. Joint consensus requires two from each three-voter set.

selfTest.q: May the leader propose new-only membership before joint membership commits?
selfTest.a: Not in this algorithm. Committing the joint entry first establishes the transition needed to rule out independent old-only decisions.

selfTest.q: Does catching up a new nonvoter increase the current election quorum?
selfTest.a: No. Replication to a nonvoter does not make it eligible to vote or count toward the current majority.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: configuration-aware quorum enumeration and a joint-transition crash trace in `loglab`; optional implementation adds serialized reconfiguration and snapshot/restart tests without changing the fixed-membership core gate.
units.stopWhen: Your quorum table rejects the union-majority counterexample and your trace identifies the configuration used at each decision; optional implementation preserves committed entries across the transition crash.

fit.note: The paper and thesis cover the required safety derivation and optional implementation omitted by MIT; the mini-project supplies explicit transition practice.

units.title: Linearizable read paths, ReadIndex and lease reads
outcomes: Derive why a leader-local read can violate linearizability after a partition.
Implement a ReadIndex path with current-term commitment, fresh quorum confirmation and an application barrier.
State the clock and leadership-transfer assumptions that lease reads add to safety.
units.why: A safe write log does not automatically give safe reads. The read must establish both authority and a sufficiently applied state while it is in flight.

next.note: Exercise read barriers against delayed replies and partitions.

study.title: Raft extended paper: read-only operations
study.locator: Section 8, read-only operations: current-term no-op commitment and heartbeat confirmation

study.title: Ongaro's 2014 thesis: ReadIndex and leases
study.locator: Section 6.4, steps 1 to 5 and follower reads; Section 6.4.1 through the clock-drift warning after Figure 6.3
study.depth: Implement quorum-confirmed reads. Derive the lease assumptions only; stop before the sequential-consistency fallback extension.

study.title: etcd v3.7: read consistency contract (page read 2026-10-15)
study.locator: KV APIs: Strict serializability, Linearizability and the `serializable` read-mode paragraph
study.depth: Use the invocation-to-response definition, not the following claim about the most current value at completion. A concurrent write need not be reflected by the read.

focus: Logging and committing a read command is a simple baseline. Bypassing the log still requires a committed current-term entry before using the leader's commit boundary.

Capture `readIndex`, confirm leadership with a new quorum heartbeat round associated with the pending read, then wait until the serving state machine has applied through `readIndex` before querying it.
Old heartbeat acknowledgements cannot certify a later read. A follower also needs a safe index from the leader and its own application barrier; merely receiving a heartbeat is insufficient.

Lease reads replace fresh communication with a timing promise. They require bounded relative clock drift, conservative lease accounting and expiry before leadership transfer; pauses and clock behavior must respect that model. Raft write safety alone supplies none of these bounds.
units.reproduce: Trace a read received after a new leader has committed a write while the old leader remains isolated: an immediate old-leader reply is stale. On the quorum-confirmed path, set the saved read index to 8 and the serving applied index to 6. Even after a fresh quorum confirms the read round, the read waits for application through index 8. Delay an acknowledgement from an earlier round and show it cannot release this barrier. Repeat with a follower as the serving state machine.
traps: Confusing log possession, commitment knowledge and state-machine application. Each is a separate prerequisite.
Treating etcd's `serializable` read option as equivalent to its default linearizable reads. It permits stale data.
Demanding the value latest at response time. Linearizability permits a point anywhere inside the operation interval, so an overlapping write can be ordered after the read.

selfTest.q: A read's quorum round finished but application is behind its saved index. Can it reply?
selfTest.a: Not yet. The serving state machine must first apply through the saved read index.

selfTest.q: Must a read include a write that completed before the read was invoked?
selfTest.a: Yes, or a later overwriting value. It need not include every write concurrent with the read.

selfTest.q: Does switching to a monotonic clock alone justify lease reads?
selfTest.a: No. Monotonicity does not bound relative rates or pauses. The lease proof needs explicit timing bounds and coordination with elections and transfer.

units.title: A deterministic message scheduler with seeded random schedules
outcomes: Drive the consensus core using explicit message, timer and persistence-completion events.
Generate bounded seeded schedules with loss, duplication, reordering, partition and restart.
Replay an explicit event history independently of subsequent random draws.
units.why: The Systems unit on distributed histories and deterministic failure simulation built the harness; extend it rather than rebuilding a broadcast harness. Consensus needs control of vote durability, log publication and stale replies as well as packet delivery.

next.note: Check each transition and reduce discovered failures.

study.title: Replicated Log and Stream Processor: fault-schedule evidence
study.locator: Architecture constraints; Milestone B - Instrumentation; Milestone D - Failure handling
study.depth: Apply these requirements only to the consensus slice of `loglab`, running locally on your machine.

focus: Make the core a transition function. Its adapter decides when messages arrive, timers fire and writes become durable; completion events must obey the persistence-before-reply contract.

Keep a stable ordering of enabled events, explicit logical time and owned random generators. A seed cannot control map iteration, goroutine races, wall clocks or external I/O that bypass the scheduler.
Give events stable IDs and retain their payloads, sender incarnation, term and prerequisites. Save the exact chosen event stream as well as seed, tool version and initial configuration.

Bound discovery campaigns. After a fault phase, include a healing phase with delivered messages, completed writes and fair timers when testing recovery; an adversarial scheduler can otherwise suppress progress forever.
units.reproduce: Extend the existing scheduler with a pending durable-write completion. Hold a vote write incomplete and confirm no successful vote reply is emitted; release completion and then permit the reply. Add a script that duplicates a message, delays its copy across a restart, partitions and heals a link. Record every chosen action and resulting core output. Run the same seed and initial state twice under one pinned Python 3 or Go version, then replay the recorded actions with random selection disabled: all three normalized transition traces must match.
traps: Recording only a seed. Code changes or an extra random draw can change the entire later schedule.
Deleting every in-flight packet on a process crash without declaring that network model. Delayed pre-crash messages are essential stale-message cases.
Calling the MIT randomized concurrent test suite deterministic replay. It is useful independent evidence, but the controlled `loglab` event model is a different test layer.

selfTest.q: Why model storage completion as an event rather than an immediate assignment?
selfTest.a: It exposes crashes and delays between changing volatile state, making it durable and sending a reply, so the ordering contract can actually be tested.

selfTest.q: Does replaying the same message sequence suffice if the core reads wall-clock time?
selfTest.a: No. Time readings can change transitions. Model time explicitly or record and replay every time input.

selfTest.q: Why add a healing phase to a recovery test?
selfTest.a: Without eventual delivery, stable participants and fair scheduling, lack of progress may be imposed entirely by the environment rather than a protocol defect.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `loglab` deterministic consensus scheduler, seeded fault campaigns, explicit durable-write completions and event-stream replay independent of the seed.
units.stopWhen: The vote reply waits for durability, delayed duplicates survive the declared crash model, and seeded rerun plus explicit replay produce identical normalized transition traces.

fit.note: The existing raft-library and DSLabs resources expose deterministic event boundaries; the project provides a named Python or Go implementation route without another runtime.

units.title: Invariant checks after every transition and failure-history minimization
outcomes: Check election, log, commitment and application invariants after every simulated transition.
Demonstrate that a planted consensus bug is detected by an independent monitor.
Reduce a violating or non-progressing history while preserving its named predicate and environmental preconditions.
units.why: The Programming unit on property, metamorphic and differential testing with shrinking taught generic shrinking. A consensus failure must retain the causal schedule and violated property, not just a failed final assertion or an opaque random seed.

next.note: Use invariant evidence to distinguish slow progress from corruption.
Extend bounded schedule exploration later.

study.title: Raft extended paper: monitor obligations
study.locator: Figure 3, all five properties; Section 5.4.3, safety argument

study.title: DSLabs: invariant search and trace reduction
study.locator: Testing and Model Checking: successor states, invariants, traces and pruning
study.depth: Study bounded exploration and witness production, not a second consensus implementation.

study.title: DSLabs: deletion-based trace minimizer
study.locator: `minimizeTrace`, `stateMatches` and `applyEvents`
study.depth: Read the repeated deletion and replay pattern. Implement your own reducer around the `loglab` event schema; no Java build is required.

focus: Maintain historical elected-leader and committed-entry ledgers outside the implementation. Checking only current roles or current logs misses a violation erased by step-down or compaction.

Check log matching on comparable retained entries and preserve enough oracle prefix data to check across snapshots. Check applied commands against an independent committed-prefix ledger, not the implementation's own commit function.

Try deleting events, replay from the initial state and keep a deletion only if the same failure predicate survives. Reject invalid replays or explicitly repair dependencies; do not accept an unrelated exception as success.

For a non-progress witness, preserve a submitted request, a reachable majority, a declared healing suffix and a fixed observation horizon. No commit by that horizon is a bounded predicate, not proof of infinite livelock.
units.reproduce: Plant a bug that permits a server to vote for a second candidate in the same term. In a three-voter schedule, give each of two candidates its own vote and let the third voter vote for both; the historical election monitor must reject the second majority. Surround the causal steps with unrelated timer and message events. Reduce the trace by deletion and full replay until no single removable event preserves the same violation. Restore the vote rule and preserve the reduced trace as a regression that no longer violates election safety.
traps: Checking invariants only after the network heals, when conflicting leaders or overwritten entries may no longer be visible.
Calling a greedy deletion result the globally shortest trace. It is only minimal under the deletion moves and validity policy you tried.
Shrinking a recovery stall into a schedule with no client request or no fair healing phase, thereby changing the question.

selfTest.q: Why record elected leaders historically instead of counting current leader roles?
selfTest.a: Two different leaders might have been elected in the same term at different moments. A current-role snapshot can hide the earlier election.

selfTest.q: A reduced trace now fails because a message ID does not exist. Is that a valid smaller consensus failure?
selfTest.a: No. It is an invalid replay unless the reducer's declared dependency policy repairs it and the original consensus predicate still fails.

selfTest.q: All sampled schedules pass. What has been established?
selfTest.a: No monitored violation was found in those bounded schedules under the stated model. This is neither an unbounded proof nor evidence for unmodeled disk or runtime behavior.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: per-transition `loglab` invariant monitors, a planted-bug negative control, minimized safety regression and one minimized bounded non-progress history with its assumptions retained.
units.stopWhen: The monitor catches the planted double vote, the reduced valid witness replays and fails only with the bug, and a separate reduced stall retains its request, healing assumptions and observation horizon.

fit.note: The paper defines the invariants and the existing DSLabs code shows executable reduction; the mini-project applies both to the learner's Raft rather than adding Paxos work.

units.title: Election, commit, recovery, message and snapshot costs and availability versus safety diagnosis
outcomes: Measure election, commit, application and recovery intervals with explicit event boundaries.
Attribute protocol messages, encoded bytes and snapshot creation, transfer and replay costs.
Diagnose lost progress separately from violated safety using histories and invariant evidence.
Compare matched fault regimes without turning local timings into universal targets.
units.why: A slow consensus group can be waiting safely for a quorum or repeatedly losing leadership. A fast one can still acknowledge unsafe work. Diagnose correctness first, then attribute the costs.

next.note: Move from one replicated log to placement across partitions.
Keep simulated, measured and proved claims distinct in the final evidence.

study.locator: Section 5.6, Timing and availability; Section 7 final two snapshot-performance issues; Section 9.3, Performance, and Figure 16
study.depth: Extract the measurement boundaries and workload setup, not the paper's millisecond values as targets.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3: cost sanity checks
study.locator: Part 3A explanation of Passed-line counters; Part 3B `TestRPCBytes3B` and `TestCount3B`
study.depth: Use the public counters as bounded sanity checks. Inspect the test code before assigning meanings to totals; printed reference timings are not targets for your machine.

study.title: Replicated Log and Stream Processor: consensus measurements
study.locator: Milestones B, D and E; Correctness requirements; Measurement requirements
study.depth: Measure only the consensus log and snapshot slice here, not the later stream-processing pipeline.

focus: Define failure-to-election, request-to-commit, commit-to-apply, request-to-reply and restart-to-catch-up separately. Logical ticks describe simulated ordering; wall-clock time measures the local implementation.

An established five-voter leader needs itself and two followers for a majority. The critical acknowledgements depend on persistence and network scheduling, not automatically the slowest follower or just one network round trip.

Count requests and responses separately from client messages, heartbeats, retries and commit notifications. Report encoded bytes as well as counts; snapshot creation, installation, transferred bytes and tail replay are distinct costs.

Use matched workload, command size, concurrency, voter count, durability mode, snapshot threshold and fault schedule. Record versions, seeds, repeated-run spread, offered work, successful work and timeouts; preserve raw histories and monitor verdicts.
units.reproduce: Construct a synthetic five-voter timeline in logical ticks, not milliseconds. The leader receives one current-term command at tick 0, persists at tick 1, then sends one append to each follower. Successful durable-replication replies arrive at ticks 3, 5, 9 and 12; no other traffic or failures occur. It can commit at tick 5, applies at tick 6 and replies to the client at tick 7. Count eight protocol messages once all four request/reply pairs finish, excluding the client pair and later commit notification. Compare these distinct intervals, then use the same event boundaries in your local measurement campaign.
traps: Reporting only successful-operation latency during a partition while omitting blocked or timed-out requests from the availability denominator.
Reducing election timeouts until one run is fast, then interpreting repeated elections under load as a safety requirement to weaken votes or quorums.
Calling catch-up complete merely when a leader is elected. A restarted node may still need snapshot installation, tail replication and application.

selfTest.q: Why does the synthetic command commit at tick 5 rather than tick 12?
selfTest.a: The leader is already durable and the second follower acknowledgement arrives at tick 5, giving three of five durable copies of a current-term entry. The other two followers are not required for that commitment.

selfTest.q: A majority is unreachable and no new commands commit. Is that a safety failure?
selfTest.a: Not by itself. It is expected unavailability under the majority contract. A conflicting application or lost committed entry would be a safety failure.

selfTest.q: Does adding a voter necessarily increase measured latency?
selfTest.a: No. It changes quorum size, order statistics and traffic, but the observed effect depends on topology, batching, scheduling and storage. Measure matched configurations rather than assert a universal direction.

selfTest.q: What should a recovery-stall report include beyond a graph?
selfTest.a: A replayable history, the bounded non-progress predicate, quorum and timing assumptions, invariant results and the event where progress resumes or its missing prerequisite.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: matched local `loglab` baseline, leader-partition, restart/catch-up and snapshot campaigns, with latency distributions, throughput, message/byte costs, timeout counts and invariant-based diagnosis.
units.stopWhen: Your dossier reproduces the synthetic counts, labels local timing distributions with their setup and spread, and explains one bounded stall without weakening the safety contract or hiding unsuccessful requests.

fit.note: The paper supplies timing and snapshot mechanisms, the lab supplies cost sanity checks, and the existing project defines the measurement and diagnosis evidence.
